Users of Mac 版 Wispr Flow can now use Notetaker—an AI-driven meeting assistant that provides more contextual information for transcripts, summaries and notes through the calendar, connected apps and personal dictionary. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker is now available on Mac

If you're not familiar with Wispr Flow, it's a leading voice-to-text AI tool for a growing number of users who are accustomed to using voice (rather than typing) to write messages, emails, documents and other texts.

Admittedly, voice operation isn't suitable in every environment. However, the user base of Wispr Flow is growing rapidly (the company said in March that monthly growth reached 40%), suggesting that AI-driven dictation tools may be becoming popular faster than many expected or imagined.

Until now, Wispr has offered only a single product that organises messy dictated content into "clear, elegant text" suitable for use across various applications.

Today, the company is expanding its product line with the launch of Notetaker—an intelligent, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcription tool and summariser. This new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new option in the app's left sidebar.

As Tanay Kothari, CEO and co-founder of Wispr, put it (no pun intended):

In other words, although transcripts themselves are of limited value to some users, accurately extracting key details, decisions and action items from them may be more practical for a broader user base.

Notetaker can also brief users before a meeting, gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line accompanied by a source link. More broadly, it pulls context from the calendar and connected apps (such as Slack).

During meetings, Notetaker provides real-time transcripts so users can quickly review what was said earlier. After the meeting, it reprocesses the entire recording with additional context, which Wispr says improves the accuracy of the final transcript, as well as the summaries, decisions, key dates and action items generated from it.

After the meeting, users can ask questions about their complete meeting notes, with answers linking to the point in time where the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also help users catch up on parts of the meeting they missed or weren't paying close attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow's custom dictionary (which improves recognition accuracy for abbreviations, names, product names, etc.), Wispr Notetaker "will reference your connected apps, such as Slack, as well as your calendar, to understand the specific context of this conversation," said Kothari.

This also helps automatically identify speakers, which is especially useful for meetings with multiple participants.

Wispr Notetaker performs transcription processing on-device and does not join calls as a separate participant, eliminating what the company calls "robots lurking in the participant list like ghosts."

It works with multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams and Slack huddles, and supports MCP, allowing users to import transcripts, summaries and notes into Claude, ChatGPT and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker launches on Mac today, with a Windows version in development.
